name: Power concentration

subjectOf.text: Concentrating too much power in any single office of a hierarchy creates a decision making bottleneck that can cripple the organization, so the tree structure that is optimal for transmitting orders downward is also its point of paralysis.
subjectOf.abstract: However, if too much power is held in any single office in the hierarchy, de- cision making finds a bottleneck that can cripple the organization.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: centralized tree structures with concentrated decision rights

subjectOf.text: The most common source of friction is the natural tendency of hierarchies to concentrate power at the top through a rich get richer mechanism: a more powerful member can use their greater power to gain still more power than a weaker member can.
subjectOf.abstract: The most common type of friction comes from the natural tendency of a hierarchy to concentrate power at the top. The basic mechanism is "the rich get richer". A more powerful member is able to use their greater power to gain more power, in any stage, than a weaker member can.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: hierarchies in which power differences among members already exist

subjectOf.text: Unchecked concentration of power drives the distribution toward one member holding nearly all resources, which is clearly inefficient for the goals of the group, and the resulting discontent is the main historical reason for revolt.
subjectOf.abstract: In the limit, if left unchecked, the most powerful member would have WXX% of the resources and the others would have X%. Clearly, getting anywhere close to this distribution is inefficient for the goals of the group. The resulting discontent is the main historical reason for revolt.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: hierarchies where the concentration of power is left unchecked

subjectOf.text: The democracy and transparency achieved by the founders of current institutions has been subverted by the natural concentration of power that evolves under competition, leaving hierarchies ossified and likely too brittle to adopt processes derived from radically different information technologies.
subjectOf.abstract: The hierarchies have ossified. They are likely too brittle now, to adopt processes that come from such radically different in- formation technologies. Changes are likely to be seen as a threat to power and re- sisted.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Future of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782201
scope_conditions: legacy institutions whose legal constitutions predate modern information processing

subjectOf.text: Once the equalizing ideal that moderates a decentralized organization is lost, competition generated by the profit motive leads inevitably to centralization with rigid rules about who holds power and wealth.
subjectOf.abstract: Without the previous equalizing ideal to moderate, the competition generated by the profit motive led in- evitably to the organization centralizing with rigid rules for who has power and wealth.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Eight Institutions for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782205
scope_conditions: organizations lacking a moderating shared ideal

subjectOf.text: Decentralized organizations can survive economic success, because current digital tools permit secure and efficient accounting of high transaction volumes so that money can be shared appropriately without centralized dictators arbitrating the dispersal of funds.
subjectOf.abstract: They allow secure and efficient accounting of voluminous transactions that happen in a decentralized network, so that money can be shared appropriately in an organization without resorting to centralized dicta- tors arbitrating the dispersal of funds.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Eight Institutions for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782205
scope_conditions: requires the digital storage, computation, networking, cryptography, and distributed computing tools described

subjectOf.text: If an organization's goal is to maintain decentralization, its tools must be used deliberately to prevent the natural concentration of power that occurs when economic inefficiencies create pockets of corruption where rent-seeking actors accumulate.
subjectOf.abstract: If, however, the goal of the organization is to maintain decentralization (assuming that is preferable), then these tools must be used wisely to prevent the natural concentration of power that occurs when inefficiencies in the economy allow pockets of corruption to accumulate rent-seeking actors.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Eight Institutions for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782205
scope_conditions: assumes maintaining decentralization is the organization's goal

subjectOf.text: Concentration of power is the greatest threat to any decentralized organization, because a single member or sub-coalition that gains a majority of power in an inherently democratic organization will eventually control it no matter what safeguards are in place, at which point the organization is no longer decentralized.
subjectOf.abstract: The idea is that if a single member, or even a sub-coalition, gains j\% of the power in an inherently dem- ocratic organization, they will eventually control it, no matter what the safeguards are.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: especially profit-devoted and therefore competitive ones

subjectOf.text: Because reputation tokens are constantly created, the reputation economy is inflationary, and a member with very high reputation must do proportionally more work merely to maintain the disparity, which makes reputation less likely to concentrate and acts as a natural counterbalance to accumulation of individual power.
subjectOf.abstract: If one member happens to have a very high reputation, they need to do proportionally more work to maintain the disparity, making reputation less likely to concentrate when people have comparable talent.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: steady state growth, not exponential growth of customers

subjectOf.text: Internal competition for profit creates a natural tendency to centralize power as members differentiate themselves through wins and losses, and this centralizing tendency is an additional destabilizing force on a decentralized organization.
subjectOf.abstract: The internal competition for profit creates the natural tendency to centralize power as the members differentiate themselves with wins and losses. This centralizing tendency is another force further destabilizing the organizations.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Governance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782214
scope_conditions: for profit organizations with internal competition

subjectOf.text: The most significant risk of bad DAO governance is centralization, in which a small group holds a disproportionate share of power or influence and thereby undermines the decentralized nature of the organization.
subjectOf.abstract: centralization, where a small group of individuals or entities hold a disproportionate amount of power or influence within the DAO, which can undermine the decentralized nature of the organization.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

subjectOf.text: Quadratic voting suppresses domination by any single participant because the cost of each additional vote rises quadratically, making concentrated control prohibitively expensive.
subjectOf.abstract: The cost of additional votes increases quadratically, making it prohibitively expensive for any one individual to dominate the voting process.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs that implement quadratic vote pricing

subjectOf.text: If a small number of hyperscale firms control electricity contracts, GPU supply chains, and data center locations, the collapse of cognitive scarcity produces digital feudalism in which abundance accrues to the controllers of the compute substrate while the rest of the economy faces artificial scarcity imposed through infrastructure gatekeeping.
subjectOf.abstract: The result would be a new form of digital feudalism in which abundance accrues to the lords of the compute substrate while the rest of the economy remains subject to artificial scarcity imposed through infrastructure gatekeeping.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Collapse of Scarcity Economics (2026). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6421319
scope_conditions: conditional on concentrated control of the physical AI substrate
